segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Working together with him, we also urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “At an acceptable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, now is the truly acceptable time; look, now is the day of salvation!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We give no cause for stumbling in anything, so that our service may not be faulted;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in everything: in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in sleepless nights, in going without food,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love without pretense,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet true,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as unknown and yet well known, as dying and, look, we live, as disciplined and yet not put to death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as grieving yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Our mouth has opened to you, Corinthians; our heart is opened wide.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are not cramped in us, but you are cramped in your own affections.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As a fair return—I speak as to children—be opened wide yourselves as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be yoked in a mismatched team with unbelievers. For what do righteousness and lawlessness have in common, or what fellowship does light have with darkness?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What harmony is there between Christ and Beliar, or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And what agreement does the sanctuary of God have with idols? For we are the sanctuary of the living God, just as God said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: Therefore come out from their midst and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will welcome you,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

notes.note: The Greek says only “working together” and names no partner. Most translations supply “with him” (God), because 5:20 has just said that God makes his appeal through Paul. It could instead mean working together with the Corinthians, or with Paul’s fellow workers.

The quotation is Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form, where God answers his servant at a time of his favor. In his comment Paul replaces the quotation’s word for “acceptable” with a strengthened compound of the same word, which “truly acceptable” tries to keep audible.

The Greek is an everyday word for service or a task carried out for someone, and it is the noun matching “servants” in the next verse. “Ministry,” used by most translations, now suggests a clerical profession, which the word did not denote.

The word normally means fasting as a religious practice, and some interpreters take it that way here. In a list of beatings, imprisonments and sleepless nights, most take it as hunger forced on Paul by his work and travels (compare 11:27). The rendering leaves both possible.

The phrase has no article and stands in the middle of a list of personal qualities, so some read it as “in a spirit of holiness,” that is, a holy disposition. Most translations take it as the Holy Spirit, which is what the same phrase regularly means elsewhere in Paul.
This may mean the message Paul proclaims (“the word of truth,” the gospel) or the manner of his speaking (“truthful speech”). Translations are divided, and the Greek allows either.

notes.phrase: the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left
notes.traditional: the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left
notes.note: A soldier carried a weapon of attack, sword or spear, in the right hand and a shield in the left, so the phrase means being fully armed for offense and defense. “Righteousness” belongs to a single Greek word-family that English splits between righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here the weapons are probably those that righteousness supplies, or that serve it.

The rare verb means to be yoked with an animal of a different kind, and echoes the laws against pairing different animals (Leviticus 19:19; Deuteronomy 22:10). The traditional “unequally” can suggest a difference of rank or strength, where the point is a difference of kind. Paul does not say which associations he means, and interpreters differ over how widely to apply it.

Beliar is a form of the Hebrew word belial, “worthlessness,” which Jewish writings of the period used as a name for the chief of the evil powers, that is, Satan. This is its only occurrence in the New Testament. Some manuscripts spell it “Belial,” the form familiar from older English Bibles.

Greek has one word for the whole temple complex and another, used here, for the building in which the deity dwells. Most translations render both as “temple.” This translation uses “sanctuary” for the second, which keeps Paul’s point that the community is the place where the living God lives.

Many manuscripts read “you are the sanctuary of the living God,” probably under the influence of 1 Corinthians 3:16. The earliest witnesses favor “we are,” and most modern editions and translations follow them.

What follows through verse 18 is a chain of scriptural phrases woven into one statement, drawing on Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27, then Isaiah 52:11, Ezekiel 20:34 and 2 Samuel 7:14, with “daughters” perhaps from Isaiah 43:6. The wording follows the Greek version freely. Because 6:14–7:1 breaks into Paul’s appeal for open hearts, some scholars think it was a separate piece placed here, while others defend it as original to the letter.
